name: Nietzsche and Machiavelli compared
plain_explanation: Russell finds a deep affinity between Nietzsche's philosophy and Machiavelli's The Prince: both propose an ethic aimed at power and deliberately opposed to Christian morality, even though Machiavelli was a practical statesman writing from direct political experience while Nietzsche was an academic philologist working out a systematic, bookish philosophy in conscious opposition to his age.
precise_definition: Russell's comparative thesis: Nietzsche's political philosophy is 'analogous to that of The Prince (not The Discourses),' sharing with Machiavelli an ethic aimed at power and deliberately anti-Christian, though worked out more systematically and over a wider field by Nietzsche, and differing in that Machiavelli was a non-systematic man of affairs in harmony with his age, while Nietzsche was a bookish professor consciously opposed to the dominant political and ethical trends of his time.
why_it_mattered: It situates Nietzsche within a longer Western tradition of frankly power-centered political ethics rather than treating him as a wholly novel phenomenon.
historical_origin: Russell's comparative analysis in this chapter.
associated_philosopher: Friedrich Nietzsche, compared to Niccolò Machiavelli
examples: Russell's formula: 'What Caesar Borgia was to Machiavelli, Napoleon was to Nietzsche: a great man defeated by petty opponents.'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Both figures' ethics are explicitly anti-Christian and power-oriented.
